stem: In a franchise agreement, who is the **franchisee**?

options.content: The person who pays to use the brand
options.rationale: Correct: the franchisee trades under the franchisor's name and pays fees.

options.content: The owner of the brand who grants the right
options.rationale: That is the franchisor.

options.content: A customer who buys from the outlet
options.rationale: Customers are not party to the agreement.

options.content: A bank that lends money to the outlet
options.rationale: A lender is not the franchisee.

explanation: The franchisee buys the right to operate under the franchisor's brand.

stem: What is a **joint venture**?

options.content: Two or more firms jointly set up a business
options.rationale: Correct: they share ownership, risk and reward of the project.

options.content: One firm buys another against its wishes
options.rationale: That is a hostile takeover.

options.content: An owner sells shares on a stock exchange
options.rationale: That is a share issue.

options.content: A business trades only for a social purpose
options.rationale: That is a social enterprise.

explanation: A joint venture is a new business jointly owned by two or more firms.

stem: Which is a **benefit to a franchisee**?

options.content: It pays no fees of any kind
options.rationale: Franchisees normally pay an initial fee and royalties.

options.content: It may change the products without permission
options.rationale: Franchisees must usually follow the franchisor's rules.

options.content: It receives a proven brand and training
options.rationale: Correct: a tested business format reduces the risk of failure.

options.content: It keeps all the profit without sharing
options.rationale: Royalties take a share of revenue.

explanation: A brand and support reduce risk, in return for fees and less freedom.

stem: What is a defining feature of a **social enterprise**?

options.content: It pays all its profit to shareholders
options.rationale: That is typical of a profit-making company.

options.content: It is never allowed to sell goods or services
options.rationale: It earns income by trading.

options.content: It trades mainly to meet a stated social aim
options.rationale: Correct: most of its profit is reinvested in that purpose.

options.content: It is always owned by the national government
options.rationale: Social enterprises can be privately run.

explanation: A social enterprise combines trading with a social or environmental purpose.

stem: A fictional pizza chain lets an entrepreneur in Gweru trade under its name, use its recipes and receive training, in return for a fee and a share of sales. For the chain, what is the main advantage of this arrangement?

options.content: It keeps all the profit from every outlet it licenses
options.rationale: The franchisee keeps most of an outlet's profit.

options.content: It can expand its brand fairly cheaply
options.rationale: Correct: the franchisee supplies the capital for the outlet.

options.content: It no longer has to protect its brand name
options.rationale: A poor outlet can harm the brand, so it must monitor standards.

options.content: It is certain the outlet will succeed
options.rationale: Success is never guaranteed.

explanation: The franchisor grows through the franchisee's capital and effort.
hints: Who pays for the new outlet?

stem: Two fictional firms, a software company in Harare and a telecoms firm in Johannesburg, set up a jointly owned company to sell a mobile payment service in both countries. Which is the **most likely** reason for the joint venture?

options.content: To remove all competition from the market
options.rationale: A joint venture does not remove all competitors.

options.content: To avoid sharing any profits
options.rationale: Profits are shared.

options.content: To make decisions faster than a sole trader
options.rationale: Joint decision-making is usually slower.

options.content: To combine technology and market knowledge
options.rationale: Correct: each partner brings strengths the other lacks.

explanation: Joint ventures pool different strengths and share cost and risk.

stem: Why might a joint venture between two firms with different management styles fail?

options.content: Joint ventures must always be run by a government
options.rationale: A government need not be involved.

options.content: Disagreements over control may delay decisions
options.rationale: Correct: clashing cultures and shared control slow decisions.

options.content: A joint venture can have no more than one owner
options.rationale: A joint venture has two or more owners.

options.content: Profits cannot be shared once a venture starts
options.rationale: Profits can be shared as agreed.

explanation: Shared control and different cultures are a common cause of friction.
hints: Consider how decisions are made when two firms share control.

stem: A fictional inexperienced owner can start an independent café or buy a franchise with high fees. Which statement is the best judgement?

options.content: The franchise is always better, whatever the fees
options.rationale: High fees could make profits too low.

options.content: The independent café is always better, as franchises fail
options.rationale: Franchises may be less risky for new owners.

options.content: It makes no difference which form is chosen
options.rationale: The choice affects risk, cost and control.

options.content: A franchise is better if its support outweighs fees
options.rationale: Correct: it sets the benefit against the cost and gives a condition.

explanation: A good judgement compares support and brand against the fees and loss of freedom.
hints: Look for the answer that gives a condition.

stem: A franchisee normally pays an initial fee and a royalty based on sales.
explanation: True. The usual fees are an initial payment and a percentage of revenue.

stem: A social enterprise does not try to make a profit.
explanation: False. A social enterprise trades and aims to make a profit, but it reinvests most of it in its social or environmental purpose.

stem: Match each term to its description.

right.content: A business set up and owned by two or more firms together
A business that reinvests most profit into a social aim
The owner of the brand who grants the right to use it
A regular payment based on a percentage of sales

explanation: Each term has a distinct meaning.

stem: Choose the correct word for each gap.

payload.template: A {{blank:a}} pays fees to use another firm's brand, while a {{blank:b}} is set up and owned jointly by two or more firms.

explanation: A franchisee pays to use a brand; a joint venture is shared ownership of a project.

stem: A fictional franchisee runs a juice bar in Gaborone. Annual revenue is US\$150,000 and costs before the royalty are US\$105,000. The royalty is 4% of revenue. Calculate the profit for the year.
explanation: Royalty = 4% × 150,000 = 6,000. Profit = 150,000 − 105,000 − 6,000 = US\$39,000. Ignoring the royalty gives US\$45,000.

stem: Two fictional firms form a joint venture and agree to share profits 55 : 45. The joint venture earns a profit of US\$60,000. How much goes to the firm with the 45% share?
explanation: 45% × 60,000 = US\$27,000 (the other firm receives US\$33,000). Sharing equally would give US\$30,000.
workedSolution: 1. 45% × 60,000 = US\$27,000 (the other firm receives US\$33,000). Sharing equally would give US\$30,000.
hints: Use the percentage that belongs to that firm.

stem: A franchisee pays an initial fee of US\$18,000 and then earns an annual profit of US\$24,000 (after royalties, spread evenly through the year). After how many months of profit has the initial fee been recovered?
explanation: 18,000 ÷ 24,000 = 0.75 years = 9 months. Using 18 or 24 mixes up the fee and profit figures.
workedSolution: 1. 18,000 ÷ 24,000 = 0.75 years = 9 months. Using 18 or 24 mixes up the fee and profit figures.
hints: Divide the fee by the annual profit and convert years to months.

stem: Name the person who owns the brand and grants the right to trade under it in a franchise.
explanation: The franchisor owns the brand and grants the franchise.

stem: Explain **two** drawbacks of buying a franchise.

points.description: Fees and royalties reduce profit
The franchisee must follow the franchisor's rules, so it has less freedom
The franchisee's reputation depends on the franchisor and on other outlets

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: A franchisee pays an initial fee and royalties, which reduce profit. It must follow the franchisor's rules on products and methods, so it has less freedom, and its reputation also depends on the franchisor and other outlets.

explanation: Any two drawbacks, developed (3 marks).
hints: Think about cost, freedom and reputation.

stem: A fictional building firm in Bulawayo is considering a joint venture with a Zambian firm to win a road contract. Explain **two** benefits of the joint venture.

points.description: The firms share the cost of equipment and finance
Application: a road contract needs expensive machinery that neither may afford alone
They share risk and combine local knowledge
Application: the Zambian firm may know local suppliers and rules

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: The two firms can share the cost of expensive road-building machinery, which neither might afford alone. They also share risk and combine knowledge, as the Zambian firm may know local suppliers and rules.

explanation: Two benefits, each applied to the contract.
hints: Link each benefit to the road contract.

stem: Analyse how being a social enterprise might affect a bakery's ability to grow.

points.description: Profit is reinvested in the social aim, so less is available for expansion
Investors may be reluctant to provide finance if returns are limited
Public goodwill and loyal customers could raise sales
Growth may therefore be slower than for a profit-maximising bakery but more stable

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: A social enterprise reinvests most of its profit in its social aim, so less is available for expansion, and investors may be reluctant to lend if returns are limited. However, goodwill and loyal customers could raise sales. Growth may therefore be slower, but more stable.

explanation: A balanced analysis.
hints: Consider the effect on finance and on customers.

stem: Evaluate whether a new, inexperienced entrepreneur should buy a franchise rather than start an independent business.

points.description: Franchise: proven brand, training and lower risk of failure
Franchise: easier to obtain finance
Franchise: fees and royalties reduce profit and the owner has little freedom
Independent: freedom and all the profit, but higher risk and no support
Counter-argument: a strong local idea may beat a franchise
Judgement with a condition, e.g. franchise is better if its fees are affordable

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: A franchise gives an inexperienced entrepreneur a proven brand, training and easier finance, so failure is less likely. However, fees and royalties reduce profit and the franchisee has little freedom. An independent business gives freedom and all the profit but with greater risk and no support. A franchise is the better choice if the fees are affordable and the brand is strong in the area.

explanation: Both sides and a conditional judgement.
hints: Compare risk reduction with cost and freedom.

stem: A fictional franchisee, Tatenda, runs a coffee outlet in Harare for a franchisor. He paid an initial fee of US\$24,000. Each year the royalty is 6% of revenue. Last year revenue was US\$180,000, cost of sales was US\$72,000 and other running costs were US\$64,000.

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Calculate the royalty paid last year.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Calculate last year's profit after the royalty (before considering the initial fee).

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: Explain **one** reason why Tatenda may be willing to pay the royalty every year.

points.description: The brand attracts customers who already know it
He receives training and support from the franchisor
Together these reduce the risk of failure and raise sales

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: The franchisor's brand attracts customers who already know it, and he gets training and support. This reduces the risk of failure and raises sales above what an unknown independent café might achieve.

explanation: Royalty US\$10,800; profit US\$33,200.

stem: Fictional Nyasha has trained as a chef and wants to open a restaurant in Victoria Falls. She has US\$20,000. The options are: (1) an independent restaurant as a sole trader; (2) a franchise costing US\$35,000 with a 7% royalty; (3) a joint venture with a lodge owner who would provide the building and share profit equally.

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Explain **one** advantage of the joint venture with the lodge owner to Nyasha.

points.description: The lodge owner provides the building, so she needs less capital
Risk and cost are shared
The lodge's guests give her ready customers

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: The lodge owner provides the building, so Nyasha needs less capital, and the lodge's guests provide ready customers. Cost and risk are shared.

parts.explanation: An advantage developed using the case.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Evaluate which option is most appropriate for Nyasha.

points.description: Independent: control and all profit, but US\$20,000 may be too little and she has no brand
Franchise: tested brand but costs exceed her savings and royalties reduce profit
Joint venture: shares cost and gives customers, but profit and decisions are shared
Criteria: finance, risk, control and her aims
Counter-argument: a joint venture depends on the lodge owner's trust and agreement
Judgement and reason

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: The franchise costs US\$35,000, more than her savings, and the royalty would reduce profit. An independent restaurant would give her control but she has limited capital and no brand. The joint venture shares cost and gives ready customers, though profit and decisions are shared. As finance is her main constraint, the joint venture is most appropriate if the lodge owner agrees clear terms on decisions and profit.

parts.explanation: Three options judged against criteria with a conditional recommendation.
hints: Use finance, risk and control as criteria.

explanation: The joint venture best matches her limited capital, if terms are clear.
hints: Which option suits her limited savings?
